meta.title: MOUD, Food, and Metabolism
meta.disclaimer: This page summarizes published research for learning purposes. It is not medical advice. Nobody should change a medication or a diet because of anything here. Talk with a prescriber, pharmacist, or dietitian.
meta.footnote: MOUD stands for medications for opioid use disorder. OUD stands for opioid use disorder. This page covers three MOUD: methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone.

strength_levels.label: Strong
strength_levels.meaning: Consistent direction across several studies, including some larger or controlled ones.

strength_levels.label: Mixed
strength_levels.meaning: Studies disagree, or results depend heavily on who was studied.

strength_levels.label: Thin
strength_levels.meaning: Only a few small studies, case reports, or secondhand reports.

strength_levels.label: Needs source
strength_levels.meaning: Not yet researched. Do not treat as a finding.

medications.name: Buprenorphine (Suboxone)
medications.note: Partial opioid agonist, often combined with naloxone. Suboxone is a brand-name combination of buprenorphine and naloxone.

medications.name: Methadone
medications.note: Full opioid agonist, usually given daily at a clinic.

medications.name: Naltrexone (Vivitrol)
medications.note: Opioid antagonist. Vivitrol is the monthly injection. Most human weight data are for naltrexone in general, not Vivitrol specifically.

cells.summary: In one small survey, people on methadone reported more eagerness for sweets and larger desired portions than comparison adults.
cells.detail: 14 methadone patients and 14 community controls answered questionnaires. Patients rated dessert, candy, chocolate, and pizza higher for eagerness, and dessert, chocolate, and candy higher for amount wanted. They also reported healthier habits than controls (more regular meals, more weight watching), which may reflect social desirability. Within the methadone group, treatment length, BMI, and food ratings were not correlated.
cells.population: Outpatient methadone patients in the US, about 50 months in treatment on average
cells.caveat: Self-report only. Patients and controls were tested in different places. Cannot separate the drug from heroin history or pre-existing taste.

cells.summary: Weight gain on methadone is reported consistently across studies.
cells.detail: A scoping review of 21 studies (16 on methadone) found that every study reporting pounds gained showed a statistically significant increase, and 9 of 11 studies reporting BMI showed a significant rise. A meta-analysis of 4 longitudinal studies (362 patients) found BMI went up in all of them. Even the largest randomized trial, which found a small change, showed a rise.
cells.population: Mostly men, many countries, many studies did not report race
cells.caveat: Strong here means the direction is consistent, not that the size is known (see the next cell). About half of the studies had under 50 people, many were uncontrolled, and some were conference abstracts. Publication bias cannot be ruled out, and studies often required patients to stay in treatment, which may select for people who differ from those who leave.

cells.summary: How much weight people gain on methadone varies widely between studies.
cells.detail: Six-month gains in the scoping review ranged from 4.2 to 23.4 lb. BMI rose 0.3 to 4.8 in the first year across studies, and a meta-analysis found 2.2 to 5.4 after at least a year. The largest randomized trial (about 500 on methadone) found about a 1.2 BMI rise in 12 months, while one 36-month US study found a 5.4 rise. US studies tended to show larger gains than European ones. Whether sex, methadone dose, cocaine use, or race change the amount is unsettled (see the Who gains more weight section).
cells.population: Mixed countries; mostly normal-weight at the start of treatment
cells.caveat: Studies used different follow-up lengths, outcome measures, and populations, so the numbers are not directly comparable. The scoping review notes that it is unknown what share of patients gain a clinically significant amount.

cells.summary: Opioids slow the gut. Constipation is a recognized problem that can reduce eating.
cells.detail: A narrative review states that opioids reduce gastrointestinal motility. A nutrition study of people with opioid dependence reported that reduced food intake was often linked to low appetite, stomach problems, and constipation.
cells.population: People with opioid dependence, not specific to methadone
cells.caveat: Comes from review statements about opioids in general. A primary study on methadone and constipation (Haber 2017, cited in Manza 2022) has not been read yet.

cells.summary: Not yet sourced.
cells.detail: To fill in: check the FDA drug label on DailyMed for food and alcohol warnings, and any interaction with grapefruit or other foods.

cells.summary: Two small studies found no difference in sweet preference between buprenorphine and methadone patients.
cells.detail: Reported secondhand in a 2022 paper: one study of 26 buprenorphine and 32 methadone patients over 2 to 3 years found no difference in BMI or sweet taste preference. Another of 19 versus 21 patients found no difference in how pleasant or intense they rated sucrose.
cells.population: Outpatients on long-term buprenorphine or methadone
cells.caveat: Secondhand. The original studies (Elman 2020, Ochalek 2021) have not been read. Also means any sweet preference on methadone may not be specific to methadone.

cells.summary: Unclear. A 12-week trial found no weight change, but other studies report gain.
cells.detail: In a re-analysis of a 12-week trial (360 people dependent on prescription opioids), average weight change was about 0.2 lb, not significant. A cohort of 107 patients reported gain over 4 months, and one case report described a large gain. A scoping review concluded there is little data supporting or refuting weight gain on buprenorphine/naloxone.
cells.population: Trial: prescription opioid dependence, US. Cohort: Turkey. The methadone studies mostly involved heroin.
cells.caveat: The trial is short and its participants differ from the methadone studies, so the two cannot be compared directly. The authors say they know of no other randomized trial of weight on buprenorphine.

cells.summary: Too little data to say. Reported amounts range from about 0.2 lb to about 10 lb.
cells.detail: The 12-week trial found an average change of about 0.2 lb. A cohort of 107 patients reported about 10 lb gained over 4 months. A single case report described a 50 lb gain in 3 months.
cells.population: Mixed; see the direction cell
cells.caveat: Only one cohort and one case report beyond the trial. A case report cannot show what is typical.

cells.summary: Opioids slow the gut in general. Buprenorphine-specific evidence has not been reviewed yet.
cells.detail: A narrative review states that opioids reduce gastrointestinal motility. It does not separate buprenorphine from other opioids.
cells.population: People with opioid dependence
cells.caveat: Stated for opioids generally. Needs a drug-specific source such as the label or Haber 2017.

cells.summary: Not yet sourced.
cells.detail: To fill in: check the FDA drug label on DailyMed for guidance on eating or drinking around sublingual doses, and for alcohol and other interaction warnings.

cells.summary: Opioid blockers reduce food intake and how pleasant food is in lab and animal work, but not hunger. Not shown in people with OUD in the sources so far.
cells.detail: A narrative review reports that nonspecific opioid antagonists such as naloxone and naltrexone reduce intake of energy-dense foods in animals and reduce palatability and intake in humans. A cited review (Yeomans and Gray, 2002) reports that antagonists reduce food intake and pleasantness in humans but have no effect on hunger, mainly for foods rated more pleasant.
cells.population: Animal models and human lab studies; populations not specified in the sources
cells.caveat: Secondhand through two reviews. The human weight data in OUD patients did not show the loss this mechanism would predict (see the weight cells).

cells.summary: The little human data show weight gain, not the loss the drug's mechanism would predict.
cells.detail: A chart review of 36 patients (20 naltrexone, 16 methadone) found no statistically different weight course between the two, and both groups gained. A case report describes a large gain on naltrexone. Naltrexone is a component of the weight loss drug Contrave, so the authors of a scoping review called these findings unexpected.
cells.population: Opioid-dependent outpatients, US chart review; one case report from India
cells.caveat: One small retrospective chart review and one case report. Not specific to the injectable form (Vivitrol).

cells.summary: In one small chart review, gain was about 10 lb over 6 months, similar to methadone.
cells.detail: Naltrexone patients gained about 4.6% of body weight at 3 months and 6.7% at 6 months, versus 1.9% and 3.7% for methadone patients. The review's discussion describes roughly 10 lb gained in both groups over 6 months. A case report describes a 33 lb gain.
cells.population: Opioid-dependent outpatients, US
cells.caveat: One study of 36 people, with no control for other factors reported in our sources. The case report cannot show what is typical.

cells.summary: Not yet sourced.
cells.detail: To fill in: check the FDA label for Vivitrol and for oral naltrexone for nausea and other stomach effects.

cells.summary: Not yet sourced.
cells.detail: To fill in: check the FDA drug label on DailyMed for food and alcohol warnings.

layers.title: Recovery phase
layers.description: Some eating changes belong to the stage of recovery more than to any one medication.

cells.title: Active use
cells.summary: Poor intake and undernutrition are commonly reported, though most people entering MOUD studies were not underweight on average.
cells.detail: A narrative review reports malnutrition prevalence of 24% to 50% in people with substance use disorders, and one nutrition study found 63% of opioid-dependent patients reported unintended weight loss. Opioids reduce gut motility. At the same time, a scoping review found that average baseline BMI in MOUD studies was in the normal range or higher, with none averaging underweight, and a 2022 paper notes obesity is less common in active OUD than in the general population.
cells.population: Mixed substances, mostly opioids
cells.caveat: Averages hide subgroups. Some samples had many underweight patients.

cells.title: Early recovery: rebound appetite and weight gain
cells.summary: Rebound explains some gain, especially for people who start underweight. But many people who start at a normal weight keep gaining.
cells.detail: A review describes rebound appetite after the suppression of active use, and a nutrition study found appetite and intake improve later in recovery. A study of 111 people in early recovery described weight gain beyond what is needed to regain pre-addiction weight. A Lebanese study of 172 men found lower starting BMI predicted more gain, but about 40% of those starting at normal weight became overweight or obese. A scoping review concluded the data partially contradict the idea that gain is mostly restored weight.
cells.population: Mixed substances; the Lebanese sample was all men
cells.caveat: Cross-sectional designs and self-reported weight limit what can be said about trajectories.

cells.title: Craving or wanting sweets
cells.summary: People in treatment consistently report wanting sweets. Most of this evidence is small self-report studies.
cells.detail: A small survey found methadone patients more eager for sweets than controls. A review describes sweet preference in people with chronic heavy alcohol use, while cocaine withdrawal may reduce the value of sweet taste, so the pattern may differ by substance. A 2023 paper notes that people in recovery show increased liking for sweet foods in human studies.
cells.population: Mixed; most direct evidence is from methadone patients or alcohol
cells.caveat: Desire is not the same as intake or weight gain. See the next two cells.

cells.title: Measured sugar intake
cells.summary: Measured intake does not clearly show high sugar. Results are mixed.
cells.detail: In a Lebanese sample, added sugar averaged only about 2.5% to 2.8% of calories and fat about 38%, based on one 24-hour recall per person. Older studies cited in a methadone survey report higher sugar intake in methadone patients than controls, but those were not read directly.
cells.population: Men in outpatient OST and residential rehab (Lebanon); older studies cited secondhand
cells.caveat: A single recall may not reflect usual intake. The older sugar-intake studies (for example Zador 1996, Morabia 1989) need to be read directly.

cells.title: Eating sweets to cope with drug cravings
cells.summary: One study tested this directly and did not find support for it.
cells.detail: In 111 people in early recovery, drug and alcohol cravings were not followed by more eating of sugar, fat, caffeine, or calories in the next two hours. If anything, people ate slightly less added sugar after stronger-than-usual cravings. A separate review uses the term addiction transfer differently, meaning difficulty telling a drug urge from hunger. The two papers are not testing the same idea.
cells.population: Mostly alcohol and cocaine, some opioids; 74% women; many in treatment for more than one substance
cells.duration: Three one-week bursts, six weeks apart
cells.caveat: One study. It measured cravings for drugs, not for food. Several results were only marginally significant.

cells.title: Does sweet desire explain weight gain?
cells.summary: Two small studies did not find that it does.
cells.detail: A thesis comparing methadone and Suboxone patients found significant weight gain on methadone and none on Suboxone, and the gain was not related to food craving, hedonic eating, or addictive-like eating. In the methadone survey, treatment length, BMI, and food ratings were not correlated.
cells.population: Outpatient methadone and buprenorphine/naloxone patients, US
cells.caveat: Small samples. The thesis is not peer-reviewed. Wanting sweets and gaining weight may both occur without one causing the other.

cells.title: Individual tendency (trait-level risk)
cells.summary: One study supports a trait-level explanation. Another found food addiction did not predict weight gain.
cells.detail: In the early recovery study, a combined score of impulsivity, low self-control, family history, number of substances, and food addiction symptoms was moderately linked to higher calorie and sugar intake and strongly linked to self-reported weight gain or appetite increase. The Lebanese study found food addiction was not associated with weight gain. The authors note that food addiction as a concept is still debated.
cells.population: Mixed substances (US); men in treatment (Lebanon)
cells.caveat: The odds ratio of about 63 is likely imprecise in a sample of 111. Some components of the score overlap with food addiction symptoms.

cells.title: Later recovery
cells.summary: Calorie and sugar intake tended to decline over months in one study.
cells.detail: In the early recovery study, calorie intake fell across the three measurement bursts and added sugar fell marginally. A sweet liking study cited by the authors found liking for sweetness decreased over time in alcohol treatment.
cells.population: Mostly alcohol and cocaine
cells.caveat: Short follow-up and many participants dropped out of later bursts.

layers.title: Setting
layers.description: Where someone lives and eats while in treatment may matter as much as the drug.

cells.title: Outpatient vs residential treatment
cells.summary: In one study, people in residential rehab reported more weight gain than people in outpatient opioid substitution treatment.
cells.detail: In 172 men in Lebanon, 78% in rehab and 54% in outpatient substitution treatment reported gaining weight (average about 10.6 kg versus 2.0 kg). Treatment type was not an independent predictor once other factors were controlled. The authors suggest, without testing it, that structured communal meals, boredom-driven bingeing, and highly processed foods served because of limited budgets may play a role.
cells.population: Men in Lebanon
cells.caveat: Weight change was self-reported. The groups differed in treatment length (5.5 versus 31.6 months), housing, and baseline BMI. The explanations are hypotheses.

cells.title: Structured meals and food education
cells.summary: Small residential programs with nutrition education or cooking activities reported better eating behavior.
cells.detail: A review describes group nutrition education in an Italian alcohol treatment center linked to more regular meals, and a 6-week education and cooking intervention across 6 men's drug treatment centers in New York that reported improved body composition and eating behavior. The early recovery study suggests handing out candy at group meetings may be unhelpful.
cells.population: Residential treatment centers, not recovery residences
cells.caveat: Reported through a narrative review. Study designs and rigor were not assessed here.

layers.title: Food access
layers.description: Money, kitchens, and food quality shape what people can eat, whatever the medication.

cells.title: Money, cooking facilities, and hunger
cells.summary: Lack of money, motivation, and cooking facilities contribute to poor nutrition in people with substance use disorders.
cells.detail: A review reports that appetite suppression, taste changes, and a lack of money, motivation, or cooking facilities all contribute to malnutrition. A Canadian study cited in the review found 65% of people who injected drugs met criteria for hunger, strongly linked to depression.
cells.population: People with substance use disorders, not specific to MOUD
cells.caveat: Secondhand through a narrative review. This is the least studied layer for people on MOUD specifically.

cells.title: Social conditions as a confound
cells.summary: People on methadone and on buprenorphine differ in employment and education, which complicates comparing the drugs.
cells.detail: A scoping review notes national data showing methadone patients are less likely to be employed and have lower education than buprenorphine patients, and that obesity patterns follow similar gradients. The authors raise this as a possible explanation for differences between the drugs.
cells.population: US patients
cells.caveat: This is a proposed explanation, not a tested one.

layers.title: Who gains more weight
layers.description: Individual factors studied so far. Most are unsettled.

cells.title: Sex
cells.summary: Findings are mixed. A meta-analysis found no significant difference between women and men.
cells.detail: Women gained more in 3 of 4 longitudinal methadone studies, but the pooled difference was not significant. In a 12-week buprenorphine trial there was no sex difference. A scoping review reports mixed findings across methadone studies.
cells.population: Mostly methadone patients
cells.caveat: The meta-analysis had only 4 studies.

cells.title: Ongoing cocaine use
cells.summary: Regular cocaine use was linked to less weight gain in a few studies.
cells.detail: In one study, people using cocaine regularly gained about 1.5 lb versus 12.4 lb in 12 months among those who did not. A scoping review reports most studies on this found cocaine use predicted less gain.
cells.population: Methadone patients, US
cells.caveat: The key studies are conference abstracts.

cells.title: Methadone dose
cells.summary: Mixed. One study found a link between higher dose and gain, two did not.
cells.detail: One study found a modest correlation between dose and BMI increase (r about 0.27). Two others found no association.
cells.population: Methadone patients
cells.caveat: Small number of studies.

cells.title: Race and ethnicity
cells.summary: Largely unstudied.
cells.detail: 14 of 21 studies in a scoping review did not report race or ethnicity. One study found Black patients gained more over 36 months than White patients.
cells.population: US methadone patients
cells.caveat: One study. Differences in access to methadone versus buprenorphine may be part of the picture.

open_questions: GI effects and food or drink interactions for each medication: use FDA labels on DailyMed and primary studies.
Vivitrol-specific effects on appetite, nausea, and weight: no sources yet.
Whether rebound appetite explains weight gain on methadone: studies rarely control for starting nutritional status.
How these findings apply to recovery residences specifically: nothing found so far.

sources.citation: Gottfredson NC, Sokol RL. Explaining excessive weight gain during early recovery from addiction. Substance Use and Misuse. 2019;54(5):769-778.
sources.note: N=111, mostly alcohol and cocaine, some opioids. Measured cravings and food intake in real time.

sources.citation: Garcia-Estrada J, et al. Malnutrition in substance use disorders: a critical issue in their treatment and recovery. Healthcare. 2025;13(8):868.
sources.note: Narrative review mixing animal and human studies. Many claims rest on secondary references.

sources.citation: Mahboub N, Rizk R, Farsoun CG, de Vries N. Patterns and determinants of weight gain among people who use drugs undergoing treatment for recovery in Lebanon. Nutrients. 2023;15(4):990.
sources.note: 172 men, cross-sectional, self-reported weight change. Use the table values for odds ratios.

sources.citation: Nolan LJ, Scagnelli LM. Preference for sweet foods and higher body mass index in patients being treated in long-term methadone maintenance. Substance Use and Misuse. 2007;42:1555-1566.
sources.note: Pilot study, 14 patients and 14 controls, data collected in 2002.

sources.citation: Manza P, et al. Sex differences in weight gain during medication-based treatment for opioid use disorder: a meta-analysis and retrospective analysis of clinical trial data. Drug and Alcohol Dependence. 2022;238:109575.
sources.note: Meta-analysis of 4 methadone studies plus a 12-week buprenorphine trial re-analysis (n=360).

sources.citation: Carr MM, et al. Weight change among patients engaged in medication treatment for opioid use disorder: a scoping review. 2023.
sources.note: 21 studies, mostly small and uncontrolled. Includes some conference abstracts. The DOI shown is the one listed for the supplementary material, so confirm it opens the article.

sources.citation: Mysels DJ, Vosburg SK, Benga I, Levin FR, Sullivan MA. Course of weight change during naltrexone vs. methadone maintenance for opioid-dependent patients. Journal of Opioid Management. 2011;7:47-53.
McDonald E. Hedonic mechanisms of weight changes in medication assisted treatment for opioid addiction. MS thesis, University of Vermont. 2017.
sources.note: Not peer-reviewed. Small subset (39 participants) analyzed for weight change.

sources.citation: Migdanis A, et al. Nutritional status and eating habits of patients with opioid dependence. Cureus. 2023.
sources.note: Title and some details were incomplete in the source text; confirm the exact title before citing.
